title: Inhouse Contract AI Use Accelerating — Survey
author: Artificial Lawyer

dom.t: Work redesign: Jagged capability demands selective deployment

st.t: Work redesign: Jagged capability demands selective deployment
st.an: The source accepts the cluster’s core model of selective, lawyer-supervised deployment and adds concrete in-house contract-work evidence: respondents report efficiency gains, support attorney-supervised first-pass review, and identify incomplete playbooks as an operating-model constraint. Its adoption and benefit figures are survey reports, however, while broader deployment is a vendor executive’s prediction rather than demonstrated organisational value.
qs: That said, only a small minority had developed the necessary ‘fully comprehensive playbooks’ required to get the most out of contract AI tools.

kp.k: Contract AI adoption accelerates among in-house legal teams
kp.d: Artificial Lawyer reports LegalOn’s 2026 survey finding that 52% of in-house legal teams are using or evaluating contract AI, with active usage nearly quadrupling since 2024. The combined usage-or-evaluation figure is distinct from active adoption. LegalOn partnered with In-House Connect to survey 452 in-house legal professionals in December 2025.
qs: more than half (52%) of inhouse legal teams already using or evaluating the technology for that use case, with active usage nearly quadrupling since 2024.
In December 2025, LegalOn partnered with In-House Connect to survey 452 in-house legal professionals.

kp.k: Respondents anticipate contract benefits and report operational gains
kp.d: The survey reports that 87% expect AI to benefit pre-signature review and redlining, alongside an average of 3.1 hours spent reviewing a contract. Separately, 79% report less time spent on routine legal tasks and 67% report faster business response and turnaround. These distinguish anticipated benefits for a specific task from reported operational improvements.
qs: 87% of respondents say AI would benefit pre-signature contract review and redlining, especially as legal teams spend an average of 3.1 hours reviewing a single contract,
79% report reduced time spent on routine legal tasks, and 67% report faster business response and turnaround times,

kp.k: Agent interest includes supervised first-pass contract review
kp.d: The survey combines adoption, evaluation and learning about agents in its 80% figure, rather than reporting that proportion as active agent users. It also finds 78% comfortable delegating first-pass contract review under attorney supervision, indicating stated acceptance of supervised delegation rather than unsupervised substitution.
qs: 80% have also adopted, evaluated, or are learning about AI agents,
78% are comfortable delegating first-pass contract review to an agent under attorney supervision.

kp.k: Comprehensive playbooks remain uncommon despite their asserted importance
kp.d: The article presents playbooks as essential to effective contract AI use. It reports that a majority had some clause library or playbook, but only a small minority had fully comprehensive playbooks, which the article describes as necessary to obtain the tools’ full benefits.
qs: The survey also looked at developing playbooks for use with AI tools, underlining how essential they were.
only a small minority had developed the necessary ‘fully comprehensive playbooks’ required to get the most out of contract AI tools.
Although, the majority did have some type of clause library or playbook.

kp.k: LegalOn CEO predicts expansion beyond contract review
kp.d: LegalOn Technologies Global CEO Daniel Lewis characterises in-house legal AI as common and its ROI as clear. Citing the report and customer feedback, he frames contract review as the gateway to adoption and anticipates expansion into daily contracting, counseling and other work. These are the vendor executive’s interpretation and outlook, not separate quantified survey findings.
qs: Legal AI has become common in-house, and the ROI is clear. Now, teams are deciding how to expand it across even more work.
This report reinforces what we hear from our customers. Contract review is the gateway to legal AI adoption, and the next phase is using AI in more daily work, in contracting, counseling and beyond.

kp.k: Author links adoption to effectiveness and changing buyer expectations
kp.d: Artificial Lawyer interprets the adoption shift as normalising AI after years of limited uptake and attributes it partly to more effective tools. The author further argues that contract review experience changes in-house lawyers’ perceptions of AI’s possibilities and may change how they view work supplied by law firms. This potential buyer-side consequence is commentary rather than a reported survey measurement.
qs: For years, tech companies have cajoled inhouse lawyers to use AI tools for contract review, but without much success.
Now, things are very different – in part no doubt because the tools are much more effective.

And while these contracts under review are perhaps not related to life or death legal matters, using AI for review changes an inhouse lawyer’s perception of what is possible, and thus it changes how they may view some parts of the work law firms do for them.

cl.s: Concrete claim or prediction about how AI changes legal services, the legal profession, or legal markets (or, for a cross-domain source, its own domain)

pts.k: The article reports rapidly rising in-house contract AI adoption and self-reported efficiency gains, while predicting broader use and possible changes in how corporate lawyers view outside counsel's work.
pts.d: Artificial Lawyer reports LegalOn survey findings that 52% of in-house legal teams use or evaluate contract AI, with active usage nearly quadrupling since 2024. It reports that 79% of respondents experience less time spent on routine legal tasks and 67% faster business response and turnaround. Anticipated benefits and openness to delegation are distinct from realised use: 87% say AI would benefit pre-signature review and redlining; 80% have adopted, evaluated, or are learning about agents; and 78% are comfortable delegating first-pass review under attorney supervision. The author interprets AI as becoming normal for many in-house lawyers and attributes adoption partly to more effective tools. The author also argues that comprehensive playbooks are needed to obtain the most benefit, although only a small minority have them. Separately, LegalOn CEO Daniel Lewis claims ROI is clear and predicts expansion from contract review into contracting, counseling and other daily work. The author suggests that using AI for contract review changes lawyers' perceptions of what is possible and may change their assessment of some work performed by law firms.

cl.s: Evidence basis offered for the claim (data, benchmarks, cases, experience, authority, or none)

pts.k: The principal evidence is a December 2025 survey of 452 in-house legal professionals; broader interpretations draw on author commentary and LegalOn's CEO's customer experience.
pts.d: LegalOn partnered with In-House Connect to conduct the survey. The article presents respondent percentages and an average of 3.1 hours spent reviewing a contract, providing context for anticipated benefits. These are survey-reported adoption, outcomes and attitudes rather than directly measured productivity or financial ROI results. The near-quadrupling claim compares active usage with 2024, but the supplied text does not give the underlying baseline or separate current active-use percentage. It refers to charts on adoption and playbooks without reproducing their numerical contents in the supplied text. Daniel Lewis says the findings reinforce customer feedback; the article provides no quantified ROI calculation. The claims that tools have become more effective and that use may alter perceptions of law-firm work are the author's interpretations, without a separate benchmark or study supplied.

cl.s: Stated or implied timeframe, conditions or qualifications under which the claim holds

pts.k: The reported change spans 2024 to the December 2025 survey; broader expansion is an undated next phase, with supervision and playbook readiness qualifying adoption.
pts.d: The 2026 article treats the December 2025 findings as evidence of a recent shift from historically low adoption. Active usage is said to have nearly quadrupled since 2024. Lewis forecasts expansion into more daily work without a deadline. Comfort with agent delegation specifically concerns first-pass contract review under attorney supervision, not unsupervised reliance. The article says comprehensive playbooks are required to get the most out of contract AI, while noting limited readiness. Its adoption measures combine different stages of engagement: use with evaluation for contract AI, and adoption with evaluation or learning for agents. The author qualifies the possible effect on law-firm perceptions by suggesting the contracts reviewed may not involve life-or-death matters.

cl.s: Who is affected and how (market segment, role, firm type, clients, or the public)

pts.k: The immediate subjects are corporate in-house legal teams and the businesses they support; outside law firms face a possible change in client perceptions.
pts.d: In-house legal professionals are described as adopting AI for contract review and redlining, reducing routine-task time, and considering supervised agent delegation. Their businesses receive reportedly faster responses and turnaround. Attorneys retain supervision in the first-pass delegation scenario. Legal teams' clause libraries and playbooks affect how fully they can exploit the tools. Lewis anticipates benefits extending into counseling and other daily work. Law firms are affected only indirectly in the author's argument: corporate clients may reassess some outside-counsel work after experiencing contract AI. The source does not make a concrete claim about job losses, fee reductions, or work actually being transferred away from firms.
